one_liner: Archived zero-copy C++17 XML parser; its old chart shows ~1.8-9x faster than libxml2 DOM but slower than pugixml and RapidXML.
what_it_does: frxml is a minimal, non-validating XML scanner: frxml::parse<callback>(std::string_view, ctx*) walks the input once and passes your compile-time callback a pointer to a temporary Element, Attribute, Text, Comment, PI or ETag record whose fields are string_views into your buffer, ending with a None marker. The parser allocates nothing; to get a tree you memcpy each record into a contiguous byte buffer, which NodeIterator walks by record size. This is the Aug-Sep 2025 rewrite; the README chart measured a deleted older API, frxml::doc, which stored the tree in one std::vector<std::variant<comment, attribute, element, pi>>, and neither API resembles libxml2's xmlDoc/xmlNode.
how_it_is_fast: It makes a single zero-copy pass that does very little per byte: names, attribute values and text come back as std::string_view slices of the input, with no entity decoding, no DTD or namespace handling, and (in the 2025 code) no end-tag matching. Delimiters are compile-time char packs (a GNU string-literal operator template plus fold expressions) and the callback is a non-type template parameter, so the scalar byte-at-a-time scan loops and the per-node dispatch inline completely; there is no SIMD, SWAR or memchr. The benchmarked 2024 code appended every node in pre-order to one geometrically growing std::vector of std::variant, where libxml2 and tinyxml2 allocate per node, which is also why it allocated less memory in the chart.
when_to_use: Machine-generated XML you control (elements, attributes, comments, PIs, plain text) where you only need to tokenize it once, and libxml2's full DOM, dictionary and well-formedness checks cost more than you need
Allocation-free or arena-style code: parse<callback> never allocates, so you decide whether to keep records, copy them into your own buffer, or drop them
Small documents where libxml2 setup cost dominates: the 2024 chart shows the widest gap over libxml2 (~5-9x) below ~20 KiB, though that was the deleted frxml::doc API
Vendoring a tiny MIT-licensed tokenizer (four headers, ~14 KB, no dependencies) that you will read, fix and extend yourself
when_not_to_use: Any case where speed is the goal and pugixml or RapidXML is an option: both were faster than frxml in its own chart (~0.8-0.9x its time, ~0.4x at 260-290 KiB)
Real-world XML with DOCTYPE/ENTITY declarations, entities (< and   stay raw), namespaces, CDATA (mis-detected, see gotchas), or whitespace around '=' in attributes (a = "x" fails with EXPECTED_QUOTE)

Untrusted or possibly malformed input: the 2025 parser does not check that end tags match (its comment says 'validation is for validator, not parser'), and the repo has no unit tests, fuzzing or CI, only a benchmark
Projects that need a maintained dependency: the repo is archived, has 1 star and no releases or tags, and its README usage example calls the deleted frxml::doc API
MSVC builds: the delimiter literals rely on a GNU string-literal operator template extension

integration.form: header-only (CMake INTERFACE target frxml; include frxml/frxml.h). The benchmarked 2024 version was a shared library.
integration.dependencies: none; google/benchmark, pugixml and tinyxml2 are git submodules used only by the benchmark
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 plus the GNU string-literal operator template extension (the code suppresses -Wgnu-string-literal-operator-template), so GCC or Clang in practice; CMake 3.27 for the repo build; compiler versions not documented
integration.platforms: not documented; portable scalar code with no intrinsics; UTF-8 input only (no BOM); both harnesses assume a Unix-like host (run.sh, and -Wl,--wrap,malloc in the 2024 harness)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; parse() has no global or static state (only a local view plus your context pointer), so parsing different inputs with separate contexts is reentrant by construction

gotchas: The code the chart measured is gone. The README figure and usage example (frxml::doc, which also references an undefined `error`) are for the Oct 2024 DOM, deleted on 2025-08-27. The head is a different callback API, and the 2025 harness that tests it has no published results.

The callback receives a pointer to a stack temporary, and each record's string_views point into your input. Copy node->size() bytes if you keep a record, and keep the input alive. Element::attrs() and children() are declared but never defined, so calling them fails to link.

CDATA detection is broken: after '<' the code matches "!CDATA[" instead of "![CDATA[", so a real <![CDATA[...]]> section becomes a bogus Element with no matching ETag. <!DOCTYPE ...> is likewise reported as an Element named "!DOCTYPE".

Header hygiene: node.h includes only <cstdint> but uses std::string_view, std::ostream and std::is_same_v, so include those headers before frxml/frxml.h. string.h defines a global SPACE macro. The CMake target calls target_compile_definitions(cxx_std_17), which defines a macro rather than requiring C++17, so set the standard yourself.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Almost never for speed. Catalogued siblings that beat libxml2 by more are RapidXml (externpro), which was also faster than frxml in frxml's own chart, and LightningXML, which also leads pugixml and RapidXML. Pick frxml only if you want a ~14 KB, allocation-free event tokenizer to vendor and extend yourself for machine-generated XML.
verified_claims_summary: The only evidence is a first-party chart (docs/Figure_1.png, Oct 2024) of the now-deleted frxml::doc DOM. It was run on pugixml-generated documents of 50-1000 elements with one attribute each and no text (about 0-330 KiB), with 3 google/benchmark iterations per size. Relative to frxml, libxml2's xmlReadMemory DOM took ~3.5x as long mid-range (~9x at the smallest sizes, ~1.8x at 260-290 KiB) and tinyxml2 ~2.6-5x, while pugixml (~0.8-0.9x) and RapidXML beat it at nearly every size. At 260-290 KiB every competitor's ratio drops at once, so frxml itself slowed ~2x in that band. frxml was built with -O3 -march=native, against distro-packaged competitors with unknown flags, and no compiler or CPU is stated. The harness's `if (!doc)` check can never fire because operator! tests an offset that is always >= 0. The legacy parser rejected character data outright (text between tags returns E_NO_BEGIN). By my reading, its tree index also left child elements out of each element's subtree size. So it did far less work than libxml2, and the result says nothing about XML that contains text.
status_note: The author archived the repo after an Aug-Sep 2025 rewrite (last commit 2025-09-02; 1 star; no issues, releases, unit tests or CI). It is MIT-licensed and the head is four small headers that are easy to vendor, but the README's chart and example describe deleted code, and the current code has the parsing bugs listed above.
